tacoma.intro: Tacoma's oldest mapped tree is the Mountaineer Tree, a Douglas fir on Point Defiance's Big Tree Trail that the city's register says has been growing since the 1500s and stands over 200 feet. The rest of this page is a single afternoon in Wright Park, where eight heritage trees from far away share one lawn: a red oak planted for Theodore Roosevelt's 1903 visit, a giant sequoia from 1939, a European and an American chestnut 25 metres apart, and a rock elm. The tenth, an American elm, stands outside the old Japanese Language School address at UW Tacoma.
tacoma.meta_description: Ten Tacoma heritage trees: the 1500s Mountaineer fir at Point Defiance, Roosevelt's 1903 oak and two chestnuts in Wright Park, and an elm at UW Tacoma.
tacoma.question_meta: The Mountaineer Tree, a Douglas fir growing since the 1500s, is Tacoma's oldest mapped tree. Free, on Point Defiance's Big Tree Trail.
tacoma.question_answer: The oldest tree mapped in Tacoma is the Mountaineer Tree, a Douglas fir on the Big Tree Trail in Point Defiance Park that the city's Heritage Tree register says has been growing since the 1500s, roughly 400 to 500 years. For a walk past several old trees at once, go to Wright Park, where eight heritage trees stand within a few minutes of each other.
tacoma.question_context:
Tacoma's trees on this page sit in three places, and none of them costs anything to visit. The oldest is the Mountaineer Tree in Point Defiance Park, a Douglas fir more than 200 feet tall with a trunk about 7.3 metres round, named in 1949 by the Tacoma branch of The Mountaineers. It stands on the Big Tree Trail, dedicated in 1955. One caveat belongs here. A local arborist has reported a bigger, unnamed fir elsewhere in the park.

Wright Park, in the Stadium District, holds the other eight within a short walk. The Roosevelt oak dates from 1903 and the giant sequoia from 1939; the tulip tree and the rock elm went in somewhere between the late 1800s and the early 1900s; the sugar maple, the pedunculate oak and the two chestnuts have no recorded planting date. The park labels more than 400 trees with Metro Parks signs, which is how you tell them apart, because every pin here comes from the city register's map and is approximate.

The tenth is an American elm on the Tacoma Avenue South frontage of UW Tacoma, which the register suggests could be 150 years old or more.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Tacoma?
faq.a: The oldest mapped here is the Mountaineer Tree, a Douglas fir on the Big Tree Trail in Point Defiance Park. The city's Heritage Tree register says it has been growing since the 1500s; other accounts give 400 to 450 years.

faq.q: Which trees can I see on one walk?
faq.a: Eight are in Wright Park, a few minutes apart: the 1903 Roosevelt oak, the 1939 giant sequoia, a tulip tree, a sugar maple, a pedunculate oak, a rock elm, and a sweet chestnut and an American chestnut about 25 metres from each other.

faq.q: Why is the American chestnut in Wright Park unusual?
faq.a: Chestnut blight killed most American chestnuts in the early twentieth century, so one with a trunk about 4.2 metres round is a rarity. It stands beside a European sweet chestnut, so you can compare the two.

faq.q: How do I find the right tree in Wright Park?
faq.a: Read the signs. Wright Park labels more than 400 of its trees with Metro Parks signs, and the pins on this page are the city register's map points rather than fixes at each trunk.

vancouver-washington.intro: Vancouver, Washington keeps two American chestnuts on the lawn of the 1878 O. O. Howard House on Officers Row, a species the city estimates is down to 300 to 500 mature trees after chestnut blight. Historical photographs suggest they grew from seed before 1890. Three more city heritage trees stand in neighbourhood parks: a black cottonwood in John Ball Park whose spring leaves scent the air, a coast redwood about six metres round beside the Burnt Bridge Creek trail, and a huge black walnut at the dead end of G Street in Arnada Park.
vancouver-washington.meta_description: Vancouver, WA heritage trees: rare American chestnuts on Officers Row, a scented cottonwood, a broad coast redwood and the Arnada Park black walnut.
vancouver-washington.question_meta: Two American chestnuts at the O. O. Howard House, likely grown before 1890, are Vancouver, Washington's oldest mapped trees. Free on Officers Row.
vancouver-washington.question_answer: The oldest trees mapped in Vancouver, Washington are two American chestnuts flanking the O. O. Howard House on Officers Row, which the city believes, from historical photographs, were grown from seed before 1890. None of the city's other heritage trees on this page has a recorded age.
vancouver-washington.question_context:
All four stops here come from the City of Vancouver's Heritage Tree Program, and all are free. The Howard House chestnuts are the reason to come. They stand one at each end of the 1878 house in the Vancouver National Historic Reserve, about a kilometre and a half east of Esther Short Park; the west tree is the larger, 27 metres tall. The city and The Historic Trust run guided tree walks along Officers Row.

The other three are neighbourhood landmarks. In John Ball Park, in the Hough neighbourhood, a black cottonwood 32 metres tall is among the largest trees in that part of town, and in spring its leaves give off a scent the city says carries for hundreds of feet. On the eastern edge of Leverich Park, cyclists on the Burnt Bridge Creek trail pass under a coast redwood with a trunk roughly six metres round. At the south end of Arnada Park, where G Street dead-ends, stands a black walnut 27 metres tall. Pins for the three park trees sit at each park's centre, so use the directions in each entry to find the trunk.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Vancouver, Washington?
faq.a: The oldest mapped here are the two American chestnuts at the O. O. Howard House on Officers Row. The city reads historical photographs as showing they were grown from seed before 1890, which makes them more than 135 years old.

faq.q: Why are the Officers Row chestnuts special?
faq.a: Chestnut blight wiped out the American chestnut across the eastern United States from the early 1900s. The city estimates only 300 to 500 mature trees remain.
No. These trees are in Vancouver, Washington, in the United States, and all four are on the City of Vancouver's own heritage tree list.

faq.q: Do I need a ticket to see these trees?
faq.a: No. The chestnuts stand on the grounds of the Howard House in the public Vancouver National Historic Reserve, and the other three are in free city parks.

salem-oregon.intro: Salem's oldest mapped tree has a park to itself. Judge William Waldo planted a giant sequoia from seed in 1872, sold his land to the city on condition the tree be kept, and in 1936 the plot became Waldo Park, about 12 by 20 feet, with Summer Street narrowed to make room. Under a kilometre away, across State Street from the Capitol, five more giant sequoias planted by Willamette University's class of 1942 form a star when seen from the centre of their ring.
salem-oregon.meta_description: Salem's giant sequoias: the 1872 Waldo Park tree in the city's smallest park, and Willamette University's five Star Trees across from the Capitol.
salem-oregon.question_meta: The Waldo Park sequoia, planted in 1872, is Salem's oldest mapped tree. Free at any hour on the corner of Summer and Union.
salem-oregon.question_answer: The oldest tree mapped in Salem, Oregon is the giant sequoia in Waldo Park, planted from seed by Judge William Waldo in 1872 and standing in a park about 12 by 20 feet on the corner of Summer and Union. The Star Trees at Willamette University, five sequoias planted in 1942, are the other stop.
salem-oregon.question_context:
Both of Salem's trees on this page are giant sequoias, both are Oregon Heritage Trees, and both are free to see in downtown Salem. The Waldo Park tree stands at Summer Street and Union Street, about ten minutes on foot from the Salem Transit Center. It is about 85 feet tall with a trunk about 22 feet round, and it has recovered from 1957, when decay took its top and several limbs. The city declared its plot a park in 1936 after the American War Mothers lobbied for it, and calls it Salem's smallest.

The Star Trees stand at the State Street edge of Willamette University, directly opposite the Oregon State Capitol. The class of 1942 gave them as a centennial gift, planted in a ring so they form a star from the centre. The state gives them about 154 feet; a local report says about 160. They are lit for a public tree lighting every holiday season, and they can be seen from the public street.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Salem, Oregon?
faq.a: The giant sequoia in Waldo Park, planted from seed by Judge William Waldo in 1872. It stands at the corner of Summer Street and Union Street.

faq.q: Is Waldo Park really Salem's smallest park?
faq.a: It is called that. The plot is roughly 12 by 20 feet, holds the one sequoia and two benches, and has been a city park since 1936.

Five giant sequoias given to Willamette University by the class of 1942 as a centennial gift, planted so that they form a star when seen from the centre of their ring. They stand across State Street from the Capitol.

faq.q: Can I visit the trees at night?
faq.a: Waldo Park is open 24 hours. The Star Trees can be seen from the public street and sidewalk, and every holiday season they are lit for a public tree lighting.
